answer: LINE (Large-scale Information Network Embedding, Tang et al., 2015) does not rely on second-order proximity to outperform graph factorization by modeling first-order proximity more effectively; the question's premise is inverted. LINE explicitly models first-order proximity (direct ties between vertices, optimized via an edge-based objective on observed links) and second-order proximity (similarity of neighborhood distributions between vertices, using a vertex and a context embedding), and concatenates the two separately trained embeddings. The reported advantage over graph factorization methods comes from scalability and from preserving these local and higher-order neighborhood structures without the cost of factorizing the full adjacency or Laplacian matrix. Second-order proximity is most useful when vertices have few direct links (sparse graphs), since two vertices sharing many neighbors are still similar even if not directly connected. The question therefore has no condition under which second-order proximity is used to model first-order proximity better; the first-order component is handled by its own objective.
